payload.name: cepstral-normalization
payload.scope: A human-made normalization procedure applied to cepstral coefficients to remove artifacts from recording conditions and channel effects, making coefficients comparable across speakers and sessions.

definition.body: Cepstral normalization is a preprocessing procedure that removes additive and multiplicative distortions from cepstral coefficients to improve robustness across speakers, microphones, and recording conditions. The two standard methods are: (1) cepstral mean normalization (CMN), which subtracts the per-coefficient mean across an utterance or session, removing static bias; (2) cepstral variance normalization (CVN), which further divides by the per-coefficient standard deviation to equalize dynamic range. Parameters: (1) the normalization scope — utterance-level, session-level, or global; (2) the coefficient indices included (typically excluding c[0] which encodes energy); (3) whether mean and variance are computed separately per coefficient or jointly. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a standard preprocessing step in speech recognition front-ends (HTK, Kaldi, librosa), specified in NIST speaker recognition evaluations, and used in all major AISI benchmark pipelines. e.g.: Kaldi's cmn() function applied to MFCC features before GMM-HMM decoding; HTK's cepstral mean normalization in the WSJ speech recognition front-end; NIST speaker recognition evaluation pre-processing of MFCC with utterance-level CMN | not: cepstral-mean-normalization; cepstral-mean-variance-normalization [formal: normalized cepstrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

payload.name: cross-phase-spectrum
payload.scope: Made so that the phase relationship between two signals can be measured and used separately from the magnitudes of their cross-spectral density, for delay estimation, phase-based coupling analysis, and phase consistency checks in system identification.

definition.body: The cross-phase spectrum is a human-made bivariate spectral measure that quantifies the phase difference between two signals at each frequency, defined as the argument of their cross-spectral density: cross-phase(f) = arg S_xy(f), where S_xy(f) is the cross-spectral density of the two signals. It separates the phase part of the cross-spectral density from its magnitude part, so that a change in relative phase between the signals is visible without being masked by a change in the magnitude of the cross-spectrum. Unlike the cross-spectrum (the raw complex conjugate product) or the cross-spectral density (which carries both magnitude and phase), the cross-phase spectrum carries only the phase angle, normalized to the principal value range -pi to pi. Unlike the phase spectrum of a single signal (arg X(f)), it is bivariate: it compares the phases of two signals against each other, not the phase of one signal against its own zero reference. Parameters: (1) the two signals being compared, (2) the spectral estimation method (direct periodogram, Welch averaged, or multitaper), (3) the averaging window length, which stabilizes the phase estimate against noise since a single-estimate cross-phase is unreliable in low signal-to-noise regions. Persistence mechanism: standardized in vibration testing and system identification protocols where the phase of the transfer function is read from the cross-phase, maintained in spectral analysis libraries (MATLAB cpsd, SciPy csd), and used in neuroscience for phase-amplitude and phase-phase coupling between signals, in acoustics for time-delay estimation between microphone or station pairs, and in seismology for inter-station phase-delay estimation. e.g.: cross-phase of a vibration transfer function read from the cpsd output in ANSI S1.11 vibration testing; inter-station cross-phase in seismological phase-delay estimation between two recording stations; phase-phase coupling between EEG and fMRI signals in AFNI fMRI preprocessing | not: cross-spectrum (the raw complex conjugate product carrying magnitude and phase); phase-spectrum (the univariate arg X(f) of one signal); coherence-function (a magnitude ratio, not a phase angle) [formal: phasium inter-signale spectrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: frequency-domain
payload.scope: Made so that a signal can be analyzed, specified, and measured by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components instead of by its waveform, giving the discipline a boundary - the frequency-versus-time split - that its curricula, standards, and instruments keep in daily use.

definition.body: The frequency-domain is the human-made representational map in which a signal is described by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components rather than by its instantaneous values in time. Signal processing and its users in communications, acoustics, and seismology draw the map's boundary: it takes in descriptions that express a signal by its frequency content - spectra, power-spectral densities, transfer functions, spectrograms - and leaves out descriptions of the signal's moment-by-moment values; the same discipline draws neighboring maps with different lines (the cepstral domain inverts the log-magnitude spectrum, the wavelet map joins time and frequency in one plane). The map's parameters are the transform convention used (continuous or discrete Fourier, windowed STFT), the axis convention (Hz or rad/s), and the representation form (magnitude, phase, power, complex). The map persists in the textbooks and curricula that teach the frequency-versus-time split, in the standards that specify frequency measurements (ANSI S1.11 vibration, ISO 16063 accelerometer calibration), in the instruments that display it (spectrum analyzers, FFT software), and in the shared vocabulary - spectrum, bandwidth, harmonic, resonance - that keeps the split in everyday use. e.g.: the frequency axis of an STFT spectrogram computed in MATLAB spectrogram; the frequency-response plot (magnitude and phase) of an LTI system in Oppenheim and Schafer DSP; the power-spectral-density plot of a vibration signal per ANSI S1.11 | not: the time-domain waveform of the same signal (the time map, not the frequency map); the cepstral domain (a map of the log-magnitude spectrum, a different representational space) [formal: regio frequentiae | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes]
